This vignette walks through how a laboratory result becomes a dossier an
epidemiologist can act on: detection, then reconciliation across runs.

## The lattice: streams, not one big feed

Every case belongs to several *streams* at once - a ward-level stream, an
institution-level stream, an area, a province, the whole catchment - each
watched independently. Streams are enumerated automatically from the
data every run, so a newly appearing pathogen creates its own streams
without any configuration step:

| Level | Unit |
|---|---|
| L1 | Ward or specialism |
| L2 | Hospital or care home |
| L3 | A contiguous geographic grouping |
| L4 | Province |
| L5 | Full catchment |

Each level is a strict partition of the one above it - a ward sits
inside exactly one hospital, a hospital inside exactly one area, and so
on - which is what makes suppression (below) meaningful.

## Four detectors, not one algorithm

- **`farrington`** (`surveillance::farringtonFlexible()`) - the standard
  statistical aberration detector for streams with enough baseline
  history, run at L1/L2 with a patient-day population offset where one
  exists, so a busy month and a quiet one at identical
  transmission-per-patient-day read as the same signal strength.
- **`same_place`** - a rule-based detector needing no baseline at all:
  *n* or more cases of the same organism at the same place within *k*
  days. This is what catches long-term care institutions, which are
  individually too sparse for a statistical baseline, and it also runs
  alongside Farrington at hospitals, where it can fire first on a fast
  cluster before a weekly aggregation has produced a point to test.
- **`rare_trigger`** - a curated list of organisms (in
  `inst/config/default.yaml`) where a single occurrence anywhere is
  itself the signal - certain notifiable or exceptionally rare
  pathogens do not need a second case to warrant a look.
- **`mem`** (the `mem` package's Moving Epidemic Method) - for organisms
  flagged `mem_applicable` (influenza, RSV), answering "has the epidemic
  started" rather than "are counts elevated", with pre-/post-epidemic
  thresholds derived from historical seasons.

A stream's own history feeds back into its baseline: a period an
assessor confirmed as a real epidemic is excluded from what
`farringtonFlexible()` sees on subsequent runs for that stream, so last
winter's outbreak does not silently raise this winter's threshold.

## Reconciliation: turning detections into clusters

Detection alone produces a burst of raised signals every run - the same
underlying cluster would otherwise appear as a new row every single
time it is still elevated. Reconciliation, run per stream immediately
after detection inside the same transaction, is what turns that into a
small number of *persistent* clusters an assessor can actually track:

1. Detections from different detectors whose intervals overlap merge
   into one candidate episode.
2. Each candidate is matched against currently open clusters in the same
   stream by interval overlap (or proximity within `case_free_days`):
   no match creates a new cluster; one match extends the existing one
   and recomputes its score; multiple matches merge, with the oldest
   surviving and the others' assessment history preserved, never
   discarded.
3. A cluster nobody's seen a new candidate for this run gets its
   `runs_since_detected` counter incremented; past a threshold, with no
   assessment ever recorded, it closes itself automatically as expected
   variation. Anything an assessor has actually classified as worth
   watching is never auto-closed - only a person closes those.

Because the anchor is the sample date, a late-arriving case can
legitimately change an already-detected signal retrospectively -
reconciliation deliberately re-runs over a rolling window, not only
"today", sized from the empirical reporting-delay curve.

## Suppression: one lattice, not five parallel views

Without suppression, one real outbreak would appear as five separate
clusters - one per level - burying the actual signal in restatements of
itself. After reconciliation:

- A child cluster suppresses its parent when it accounts for most of the
  parent's excess (the rise is local; the wider view adds nothing).
- A parent suppresses its children when the rise is spread across
  several of them with no single dominant one (the rise is diffuse;
  five separate area-level clusters would just be noise).
- The suppressed clusters are never discarded - they stay attached as
  context, visible on the surviving cluster's detail screen.

## Derived state, not a stored status

A cluster's displayed state (new, assessing, monitoring, ready to close,
closed, needs reassessment) is *computed*, every time, from its
classification history, the case-free clock, and whether it changed
since it was last assessed - never stored and hand-edited. See
`episode_derive_state()` for the exact rule and `state_derive.R`'s own
tests for every transition it covers.
